summary: Describes RSVP-TE procedures and extensions for setting up and maintaining label switched paths that cross domain boundaries, in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic-engineered path in MPLS often has to cross more than one network, such as two autonomous systems. This document says what the router at the border between two networks must do when the setup request arrives: check policy, pick how to carry the path across its own network, and keep the other networks from learning too much about its inside. It also adds one flag the starting router can set to insist that the whole path be set up as a single path.

questions: what is the contiguous lsp bit
contiguous vs nested vs stitched lsp
subtitle: How a traffic-engineered MPLS or GMPLS path can be signaled across several networks, and how the start of the path can insist on one method.

tldr.problem: A traffic-engineered Label Switched Path often has to cross several domains, such as Autonomous Systems or IGP areas, each with its own policies and path computation. RSVP-TE alone does not say how the border nodes should handle that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the procedures a domain border node follows for policy, signaling method, ERO processing, crankback and RRO filtering. It adds one flag bit, the Contiguous LSP bit, so the ingress can forbid nesting and stitching.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a defined way to choose between contiguous, nested and stitched LSPs per domain, with new error codes for policy and method conflicts. It updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

today: RFC 5151 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. It updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and the Three Signaling Methods
sections.content:
The requirements for inter-area and inter-AS Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering are stated in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, and many of them also apply to Generalized MPLS networks. The framework for inter-domain MPLS-TE is provided in RFC 4726.

This document presents procedures and extensions to RSVP-TE signaling for the setup and maintenance of traffic engineered label switched paths that span multiple domains in MPLS-TE or GMPLS networks. The procedures apply to MPLS-TE packet LSPs established with RSVP-TE and to all LSPs, packet or not, that use the RSVP-TE GMPLS extensions.

For this document, a domain is any collection of network elements within a common realm of address space or path computation responsibility. Examples are Autonomous Systems, IGP routing areas and GMPLS overlay networks.

Three signaling methods for inter-domain RSVP-TE signaling are identified in RFC 4726. Contiguous LSPs are achieved with the procedures of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473 to create a single end-to-end LSP that spans all domains. Nested LSPs are established with the techniques of RFC 4206, which carry the end-to-end LSP inside a separate tunnel across each domain. Stitched LSPs are established with the procedures of RFC 5150, which build an end-to-end LSP from the concatenation of separate LSPs each spanning a domain.

This document defines the RSVP-TE protocol extensions needed to control and select which of the three mechanisms is used for any one end-to-end inter-domain TE LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic-engineered path has to cross networks that are administered separately. There are three ways to build it, and the router at the border decides which one to use for its own network. This document describes those choices and the rules the border router follows.

sections.title: How the Three Methods Differ
sections.content:
A contiguous TE LSP is a single TE LSP set up across multiple domains using the RSVP-TE procedures. No additional TE LSPs are required, and the same RSVP-TE information for the TE LSP is maintained along the entire path. In particular, the TE LSP has the same RSVP session and LSP ID at every LSR along its path.

With nesting, one or more TE LSPs are nested within another TE LSP, as described in RFC 4206. The technique can nest one or more inter-domain TE LSPs into an intra-domain hierarchical LSP, or H-LSP, and label stacking is used to achieve nesting in packet networks. The document uses H-LSP for an LSP that allows other LSPs to be nested within it. An H-LSP may be advertised as a TE link within the same instance of the routing protocol that was used to advertise the TE links it was created from, in which case it is a Forwarding Adjacency.

With stitching, as described in RFC 5150, shorter LSP segments are joined to create a single longer LSP. The segments of an inter-domain LSP may be intra-domain LSPs or inter-domain LSPs. Stitching in the data plane results in a single end-to-end contiguous LSP, but in the control plane each segment is signaled as a separate LSP with distinct RSVP sessions, and the end-to-end LSP is signaled as yet another LSP with its own RSVP session. The control plane operation for stitching is therefore very similar to that for nesting.

Any combination of the three options may be used in the course of one end-to-end inter-domain LSP, because they are per-domain transit options. The choice is a matter of policy for the node requesting the setup and policy for each successive domain border node. The decision whether to signal contiguously, or to nest or stitch, depends on the parameters signaled from the ingress node and on the configuration of the local node. The stitching segment or H-LSP used to cross a domain may be pre-established or signaled dynamically in response to the arriving setup request.

An implementation of a transit LSR is unaware of the options, because it sees only TE LSPs. An implementation of a domain border LSR has to decide which mechanisms of inter-domain support to include, but must in any case support contiguous inter-domain TE LSPs, since that is the default mode of operation for RSVP-TE. Failing to support nesting or stitching restricts the operator's options but does not prevent the establishment of inter-domain TE LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Contiguous means one LSP from end to end, with the same session identifier at every hop. Nested means the end-to-end path rides inside another path that the domain builds for itself. Stitched means the domain builds its own segment and the segments are joined together. In the control plane, nested and stitched look similar: the end-to-end path is a separate LSP from the ones underneath it.

sections.title: Procedures on the Domain Border Node
sections.content:
Whether an inter-domain TE LSP is contiguous, nested or stitched is limited by the signaling methods supported by or configured on the intermediate nodes. The restriction usually applies at the domain border nodes, since other transit nodes are oblivious to the mechanism in use. The ingress of the LSP may further restrict the choice by setting parameters in the Path message.

When a domain border node receives the RSVP Path message for an inter-domain TE LSP setup, it MUST carry out the following procedures before forwarding the Path message to the next node along the path.

First, it applies the policies of the domain and of the node itself, which may restrict the establishment of inter-domain TE LSPs. On a policy failure the node SHOULD fail the setup and send a PathErr with the error code "Policy control failure" and the value "Inter-domain policy failure".

Second, it determines the signaling method used to cross the domain. Restrictions specified by the ingress node MUST be adhered to, and within the freedom the ingress allows, the border node MAY choose any method according to its local configuration and policies. If no resulting signaling method is available or allowed, the border node MUST send a PathErr as described later in the document. The document gives the case where an ingress asks for a contiguous LSP because it wants maximum control over the path and over when reoptimization happens, while the operator of a transit domain allows only stitching so that it can reoptimize its own domain under its own control. The policy applied at the entry to the transit domain then returns a PathErr, and the ingress has three choices: find another path that avoids the transit domain, relax its requirements, or fail to provide the service.

Third, it carries out the ERO procedures, in addition to the procedures of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. Fourth, it performs any path computations needed to determine the path across the domain and potentially the exit point from the domain. The path computation procedure is outside the scope of the document; a path computation option is specified in RFC 5152 and another option is to use a Path Computation Element in RFC 4655. In the case of nesting or stitching, the node either finds an existing intra-domain TE LSP to carry the inter-domain TE LSP or signals a new one, depending on local policy. On a path computation failure the node SHOULD send a PathErr with the error code "Routing Problem" and a value chosen for the reason of the failure, though it MAY opt to discard the Path message silently instead.

On the receipt of a PathErr reporting a signaling failure from within the domain or from a downstream domain, the border node MAY apply the crankback procedures of RFC 4920. If crankback is not applied or is exhausted, the border node MUST continue with the PathErr processing of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473. On the successful processing of a Path or Resv message, the border node MUST carry out the RRO procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: When the setup request reaches the border router, it checks its own policy, decides which of the three methods to use for the domain it sits on, processes the explicit route, and computes the path if it needs to. If the setup later fails, it may try to re-route around the failure before passing the error on.

sections.title: ERO Processing, Crankback and the Record Route
sections.content:
The explicit route a border node receives in the Path message was supplied by the ingress node and may have been updated by other nodes as the message was propagated. Its content depends on the path computation techniques used, the degree of traffic engineering visibility available to the nodes computing the path, and the policy of the nodes that created or modified it. The rules that follow may be applied at any node within a domain, although the term domain border node is kept for clarity.

The document gives six rules for ERO processing. Any policies related to ERO processing MUST be applied, for example a policy to reject EROs that identify nodes inside the domain; on a failure the node SHOULD issue a PathErr with the error code "Policy control failure" and the value "Inter-domain explicit route rejected", though it MAY be configured to discard the Path message silently or to return a different error code for security reasons. The procedures of Section 8.2 of RFC 4206, which describe how a node at the edge of a region processes the ERO and uses it to find an existing H-LSP or signal a new one, MUST be followed for nesting or stitching.

If an ERO subobject identifies a TE link formed by the advertisement of an H-LSP or LSP segment, whether numbered or unnumbered, contiguous signaling MUST NOT be used. The node MUST use either nesting or stitching, according to the capabilities of the LSP that forms the TE link, the parameters signaled in the Path message and local policy. If there is a conflict, the node SHOULD send a PathErr with the error code "Routing Problem" and the value "ERO conflicts with inter-domain signaling method", with the same option to discard silently.

An ERO received by a border node may have a loose hop as the next hop, which may be an IP address or an AS number. The ERO MUST then be expanded to determine the path to the next hop, using some form of path computation that may itself generate loose hops. In the absence of any ERO subobjects beyond the local border node, the LSP egress, the destination encoded in the RSVP Session object, MUST be considered the next loose hop and the same rule applied. On any other failure processing the ERO, a PathErr SHOULD be sent as described in RFC 3209 or RFC 3473, and again the node MAY be configured to discard the Path message silently or to return a different error code for security reasons.

When an error occurs during LSP setup, a PathErr is sent back towards the ingress, and if the LSP traverses multiple domains the PathErr is seen successively by each border node. Border nodes MAY apply local policies to restrict the propagation of information about the contents of the domain, for example by replacing the information that indicates a specific failure at a specific node with a more general error covering the whole domain. A border node MUST NOT suppress the propagation of a PathErr, except to attempt rerouting as described here. Nodes other than border nodes SHOULD NOT modify the contents of a PathErr, and border nodes SHOULD NOT modify them unless domain confidentiality is a specific requirement.

Border nodes are an opportunity for crankback rerouting. On receipt of a PathErr caused by a setup failure, a border node MAY hold the PathErr and make further attempts to establish the LSP, if local policy and the parameters signaled on the Path message allow it. Such attempts might involve computing alternate routes through the domain or selecting different downstream domains. If a subsequent attempt succeeds, the border router MUST discard the held PathErr; if all attempts fail, it MUST send the PathErr upstream towards the ingress, and it MAY change the information in the message to provide further crankback details and aggregation. Crankback rerouting MAY also be used for the failure of LSPs after they have been established.

The record route object, defined in RFC 3209 as an optional object used for loop detection and for information about the hops traversed, may be filtered or modified by a border node for confidentiality reasons according to local policy. A series of identifiers of hops within a domain MAY be replaced with the domain identifier, such as the AS number, or removed entirely, leaving only the domain border nodes. A border router MUST NOT mask its own presence and MUST include itself in the record route. Filtering does not hamper the signaling protocol, but the information loss may make management diagnostic procedures inoperable or more complicated, and procedures that depend on record route information may become less efficient, as the Fast Reroute procedures of RFC 4090 use it to determine labels and the downstream merge point.

Notify messages, introduced in RFC 3473, may be sent directly rather than hop by hop and so may speed the propagation of error information. If a border router wants to see them, for example to provide protection switching, it is RECOMMENDED that it update the Notify Request objects in the Path and Resv messages to show its own address. The replacement of a notify recipient means that some Notify messages may need to be examined, processed and forwarded at domain borders, a trade-off in which the cost increases linearly with the number of domains in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The explicit route is the list of hops the path should follow. The border router applies six rules to it, including one that forces nesting or stitching when the route names a path the domain itself built. It may hide the inside of its domain from the rest of the network, but it must not hide itself, and it must not swallow the error report.

sections.title: The Contiguous LSP Bit
sections.content:
In many network environments there is a network-wide policy that determines which of the three inter-domain LSP techniques is used, and in that case no protocol extension is needed. In environments that support more than one technique, an ingress node may wish to constrain the choice made by border nodes for each inter-domain TE LSP it originates.

The LSP_Attributes object defined in RFC 4420 can be used to signal required attributes of an LSP, and its Attributes Flags TLV includes Boolean flags that define individual attributes. This document defines a new bit, the Contiguous LSP bit, that the ingress node can set to restrict the intermediate nodes to using contiguous signaling. The flag is set by the ingress node that originates a Path message to set up an inter-domain TE LSP when it requires the contiguous LSP technique, and it is only to be used in the Attributes Flags TLV.

When a domain border LSR receives a Path message with this bit set to one, it MUST NOT perform stitching or nesting for that setup. When the bit is clear, the border LSR MAY perform stitching or nesting according to local policy. The bit MUST NOT be modified by any transit node.

An intermediate node that supports the LSP_Attributes object and the Attributes Flags TLV and also recognizes the Contiguous LSP bit, but cannot support contiguous TE LSPs, MUST send a Path Error message with the error code "Routing Problem" and the value "Contiguous LSP type not supported". A node that recognizes the object, the TLV and the bit and also supports the desired behavior MUST signal a contiguous LSP, and if it is a domain border node, or if it expands a loose hop in the ERO, it MUST include an RRO Attributes subobject in the record route of the corresponding Resv message, if that object is present, with the Contiguous LSP bit set to report its behavior. Domain border LSRs MUST support and act on the setting of the flag.

A node that supports the LSP_Attributes object but does not recognize the Attributes Flags TLV, or supports the TLV but does not recognize the Contiguous LSP bit, MUST forward the object unmodified. What the ingress does with a PathErr received when it asked for a contiguous LSP is out of the scope of the document, but may include computing an alternate path.
sections.plainLanguage: The one new piece of signaling is a single bit in the attributes of the setup request. When it is set, every border router must build one continuous path and may not use its own nested or stitched path. The bit is never changed in flight, and a router that does not understand it passes it on unchanged.

sections.title: Protection and Recovery of Inter-Domain TE LSPs
sections.content:
The procedures of the earlier sections MUST be applied to all inter-domain TE LSPs, including bypass tunnels, detour LSPs of RFC 4090 and segment recovery LSPs of RFC 4873, so these LSPs are also subjected to ERO processing, policies and path computation. The paths for the backup LSPs need to be pre-configured and signaled with the protected LSP, or computed on demand at the point of local repair. As with any inter-domain TE LSP, the ERO may comprise strict or loose hops and depends on the traffic engineering visibility the computation point has into the next domain.

If loose hops are present in the path of the backup LSP, ERO expansion will be required somewhere along the path, probably at a border node. To keep the backup path disjoint from the protected LSPs, the node performing the expansion must be given the path of the protected LSPs between the point of local repair and the merge point. That information can be gathered from the record routes of the protected LSPs and is signaled in the DETOUR object for Fast Reroute, and route exclusion is used for other protection schemes.

Fast Reroute describes two methods for local protection of a packet TE LSP in case of link, shared risk link group or node failure. Within a domain, the mode of operation to protect a contiguous, stitched or nested TE LSP is identical to the existing procedures, and in the case of nesting or stitching the end-to-end LSP is automatically protected by the protection operation performed on the H-LSP or the stitching segment LSP. No protocol extensions are required.

Where two domains are connected by a TE link, each domain has its own border node and the two are connected by that link. A contiguous LSP can be backed up using any point of local repair and merge point, but if the LSP uses stitching or nesting in either connected domain, those two roles MUST be held by the border nodes of those domains, and it will usually be the border nodes connected by the failed link that are used. To protect an inter-domain link with Fast Reroute, a set of backup tunnels must be configured or dynamically computed between the point of local repair and the merge point so that they are diversely routed from the protected inter-domain link and the protected inter-domain LSPs. Each protected inter-domain LSP using that link must be assigned to a next-hop bypass tunnel diverse from the protected LSP, and such a tunnel can be selected by analyzing the record routes in the Resv messages of the available bypass tunnels and of the protected TE LSP.

For the failure of a border node, if stitching or nesting is used the failed node will be the start or the end, or both, of a stitching segment LSP or an H-LSP, so protection must be provided to the far end of that segment or H-LSP. The point of local repair is then the upstream domain entry point in the case of failure of the domain exit point, and the merge point is the downstream domain exit point in the case of failure of the domain entry point. Where the border falls at a single border node, both cases apply. If the contiguous LSP mechanism is in use, normal selection applies and any node within the domains may fill these roles. Where the point of local repair is not immediately upstream of the failed node, error propagation time may be delayed unless a mechanism such as BFD for MPLS is implemented or direct reporting is employed, for example through the GMPLS Notify message.

GMPLS-based segment recovery allows protection against a span failure, a node failure or failure over any particular portion of a network used by an LSP. The domain border failure cases can occur in GMPLS networks too and can be protected against using segment protection without additional protocol extensions. If loose hops are used in the construction of the working and protection paths for segment protection, care is required to keep the paths disjoint. If the paths are signaled incrementally, route exclusion may be used to ensure that they are disjoint; otherwise a coordinated path computation technique such as cooperating Path Computation Elements can provide suitable paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The same rules apply to the backup paths: they cross domains too, so the border routers process them the same way. When a link between two domains fails, the backup path has to be built so that it avoids that link, and the routers that build it need to know the path of the protected path so the two stay apart.

sections.title: Reoptimization and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Reoptimization is the process of moving an LSP from its current path to a more preferred path, involving the determination of the preferred path and make-before-break signaling procedures to minimize traffic disruption. Reoptimization of an inter-domain TE LSP may require a new path in more than one domain.

The nature of the inter-domain setup mechanism determines how reoptimization can be applied. If the LSP is contiguous, the make-before-break signaling MUST be initiated by the ingress node. If reoptimization is limited to a change within one domain, that is, if there is no change to the domain border nodes, and nesting or stitching is in use, the H-LSP or stitching segment may be reoptimized independently inside the domain without affecting the end-to-end LSP.

The ingress LSR may still wish to exert control and coordination over the process. A transit domain may know that reoptimization is possible but not bother, because it is not worried about the level of service across the domain, while the cumulative effect on the end-to-end LSP may make the head end want to trigger an end-to-end reoptimization request, which the transit domain may ignore. End-to-end reoptimization also has an advantage over per-domain reoptimization for non-contiguous inter-domain LSPs, because per-domain reoptimization is restricted to preserving the domain entry and exit points, since changing them would break the LSP, while end-to-end reoptimization can select new border routers.

There are cost and benefit considerations between the two. The greater the number of hops involved in the reoptimization, the higher the risk of traffic disruption, and the shorter the segment reoptimized, the lower the chance of a substantial improvement in the end-to-end LSP. Administrative policies should be applied in this area with care.

The mechanisms of RFC 4736 allow the ingress node to request each node with a loose next hop to re-evaluate the current path in search of a better one, and allow a node with a loose next hop to inform the ingress node that a better path exists. These SHOULD be used for reoptimization of a contiguous inter-domain TE LSP. Because end-to-end reoptimization may involve a non-local modification that selects new entry or exit points, local reoptimization is more easily achieved with nesting or stitching, and the locality principle, the idea of keeping information only where it is needed, is best achieved that way. A contiguous LSP can also be modified to take advantage of local reoptimization, even if that requires the dissemination of information and signaling outside the local domain.

The procedures are backward compatible with existing deployments. Ingress LSRs are not required to support the extensions to provision intra-domain LSPs, and the default behavior of a transit LSR that receives a Path message without the Contiguous LSP bit set, or without the object at all, is to allow all modes of inter-domain TE LSP, so older ingress LSRs can still initiate inter-domain LSPs. Transit, non-border LSRs are not required to perform any special processing and pass the LSP_Attributes object on unmodified, so older transit LSRs are fully supported. Domain border LSRs do need to be upgraded before inter-domain TE LSPs are allowed, because policy, administrative and security controls have to be established before permitting LSPs to be signaled across a domain border. The record route additions are fully backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving an established path to a better route can be done for the whole path at once or for one domain at a time. Doing it per domain is easier but cannot change the points where the path enters and leaves each domain. Existing deployments keep working: old transit routers pass the new information along unchanged, and only border routers have to be upgraded.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP does not currently provide for automated key management, and RFC 4107 states a requirement for mandatory automated key management under certain situations. The document notes that work is starting in the IETF to define improved authentication, including automated key management for RSVP, and that implementations and deployments should pay attention to the results.

Before electing to use inter-domain signaling for MPLS-TE, the administrators of neighbouring domains MUST satisfy themselves that a suitable trust relationship exists between the domains. In the absence of such a relationship, they SHOULD decide not to deploy inter-domain signaling and SHOULD disable RSVP-TE on any inter-domain interfaces.

An operator may make use of the security features already defined for RSVP-TE, which may require coordination between the domains to share keys, and care is required to ensure the keys are changed sufficiently frequently. This may involve additional synchronization if the border nodes are protected with Fast Reroute, since the merge point and the point of local repair should also share the key.

For an inter-domain TE LSP, especially when it traverses different administrative or trust domains, the document says the following mechanisms SHOULD be provided to an operator. There should be a way to enforce policies and filters at the domain borders to process incoming setup requests based on agreed trust and service levels between domains, where various LSP attributes such as bandwidth and priority could be part of the contract. There should be a way to rate-limit LSP setup requests or error notifications from a particular domain. There should be a mechanism for policy-based outbound RSVP message processing at the border node, which may involve filtering or modification of certain addresses in RSVP objects and messages.

An operator may also wish to reduce the signaling interactions between domains. For example, the operator might not trust the neighbouring domain to supply correct or trustable restart information, and might ensure the availability of the restart function is not configured in the Hello message exchange across the domain border. Suitable configuration MUST therefore be provided so that the operator can control optional protocol features that may be considered a security risk.

The document gives examples of such policies. An operator may implement ERO filtering on the border node to disallow hops inside the domain from being identified in the ERO of an incoming Path message, either by rejecting the Path message or by ignoring the hops inside the domain. To preserve the confidentiality of the network topology, an operator may disallow recording hops inside the domain in the record route, or filter out recorded record route addresses at the border node. An operator may require the border node to modify the addresses of messages such as PathErr or Notify originated from hops inside the domain. And on a path computation failure, an operator may require the border node to silently discard the Path message instead of returning a PathErr, because a Path message could be interpreted as a network probe and a PathErr provides information about the network capabilities and policies.

Operations, administration and management mechanisms such as BFD for MPLS and RFC 4379 are commonly used to verify the connectivity of end-to-end LSPs and trace their paths. Where the LSPs are inter-domain, such techniques MAY require the messages to be intercepted or modified at domain borders, or passed transparently across domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbouring networks have to trust each other before they set up paths for each other, and if they do not, they should not turn RSVP-TE on between them. The document lists what an operator should be able to do at the border: apply policies to incoming setup requests, limit how many requests a neighbour can send, filter the other network's hops out of the path, and hide the addresses of internal hops in error reports.

viz.caption: THE THREE INTER-DOMAIN SIGNALING METHODS OF RFC 5151

cells: One TE LSP set up across multiple domains
Same RSVP session and LSP ID at every LSR on the path
One or more TE LSPs nested inside another TE LSP
Label stacking in packet networks; the carrying LSP is an H-LSP
Separate LSP segments, each spanning a domain
Each segment has its own RSVP session, plus one for the end-to-end LSP

viz.caption: THE PER-DOMAIN EXAMPLE FROM RFC 5151, SECTION 2
WHAT THE DOMAIN BORDER NODE DOES WITH A SETUP REQUEST

items.title: Apply policy
items.text: Fail the setup with an inter-domain policy failure if the domain refuses it.

items.title: Choose the method
items.text: Contiguous, nested or stitched, within the limits the ingress set.

items.title: Process the ERO
items.text: Apply the explicit route rules, expanding loose hops where needed.

items.title: Compute the path
items.text: Find the path across the domain and, with nesting or stitching, the carrying LSP.

items.title: Report the record route
items.text: Filter the hops inside the domain, but always include the border node itself.
